s: Amos 3:3 — “Can two people walk together unless they agree?”
In the Bible, we often find a “no” statement written in the form of a question.
Our text is an example of this. So we should understand the prophet to be saying that two people cannot walk together unless they agree.
For two people to agree means more than agreeing in their ideas or their understanding. We often see people who agree in their beliefs but are very different in how they feel and how they live.
Their minds may accept the same truths, while those truths affect their hearts and actions in very different ways.
Saints and sinners often hold the same religious beliefs on paper. Yet it is clear that they are very different in how they feel and live.
We have reason to believe that holy angels and demons understand and accept the same truths in their minds. And yet how differently those truths affect them!
The same truths have different effects on different minds. This happens because each person’s heart, or feelings, are in a different state.
To put it another way, the difference lies in how each person receives these truths—how they feel and act because of them.
We should also notice that the same things and truths will affect the same person very differently at different times.
This, too, comes from the different state of that person’s feelings at those times.
Or, to say it better, this difference lies in the different way the mind is acting at those times.
All pleasure and pain, all happiness and misery, all sin and holiness, live in the heart and its feelings. That is where they belong.

Whenever a truth or a thing is put before our minds, we feel either satisfied or dissatisfied, pleased or pained. That reaction depends completely on the state of our feelings at that moment. In fact, the reaction is made up of those feelings.
If the thing matches our feelings, and stirs them up and feeds them in a pleasant way, of course we are pleased. That is because our pleasure and happiness are made of those pleasant feelings.
So the higher something lifts these feelings when it is put before our minds, the greater our pleasure is.

But if the thing or truth does not match our feelings, it cannot please us. Suppose it is off to the side of what we are feeling right now, and we refuse to change the direction of our feelings. Then one of two things will happen. Either we will not care about it, because our feelings are busy with something else. Or, if it keeps pushing on us, we will turn away from it and resist it.
Now suppose it is not only off to the side of what we care about right now, but actually against it. Then, as long as our feelings stay the same, we will—and must—resist it and fight it.

Sometimes a subject is brought up and pushed on us that is different from the one our feelings are caught up in. Then we feel bored, or even annoyed and disgusted. But that is not all. Even on the same subject, something may be presented that is far above or far below the level of our feelings. If our feelings stay the same, and we refuse to be drawn in and lifted to that level, we will feel bored—and perhaps hurt and offended.

Suppose the subject is shown in a way that is below the level of our present feelings. Then we cannot be interested until it comes up to our level. And suppose the subject keeps being held before us in this cooling way, which seems cheap to us, while we are struggling to keep our high feelings. Then we become unhappy, because our feelings are not being fed. They are being fought.

Now suppose the subject is presented in a way that is far above the level of our feelings, and our feelings stay low and refuse to rise. Then it does not match or feed our feelings, so we cannot be interested. It seems like wild fanaticism to us. We are annoyed by the warmth we do not choose to share. And the higher it is above our own temperature, the more disgusted we are.
Everyone’s experience will prove these things true. They hold true on every subject and in every situation, because they are based on principles built into human nature itself.

Take a passionate politician. Talk to him about his favorite subject, in the way he likes best. Once his feelings are caught up in it, add the fire of powerful speaking. Make it burn and blaze in his mind, and you will delight him greatly.
But change your style and tone. Turn down your fire and feeling. Turn the subject over. Present it in a drier way. At once he loses almost all his interest and becomes uneasy as things go downhill.
Now change the subject. Bring up death and the solemn judgment. He is shocked and stunned. Keep pressing him with them, and he is disgusted and offended.

Why does he lose interest in his favorite subject? It is the natural result of taking away the burning picture of it that was pouring fire through his feelings. Why is he disgusted when you change the subject? It is the natural result of putting in front of him something that went directly against the way he felt at that moment.
Unless he chooses to turn his mind along with you as you change the subject, he cannot help being displeased.
Picture a trained musician listening, almost carried away with joy, as a beautiful piece of music is played with great skill.
Now throw some clashing, off-key notes at him. In a moment he is in pain.
Make the harsh sounds louder and longer, and he walks out of the room in disgust.

Or imagine this. You love music, but right now you are sad. You are going through great trouble, and you feel like crying. The gentle, mournful sound of a wind harp drifts softly to your ears and seems to melt around your heart. Your tears flow fast. But then the racket of trumpets, drums, and cymbals bursts in, along with a shrill fife playing a cheerful, quick march. It drowns out the soft whispers of the harp. You feel upset. You turn away and cover your ears.
The mournful harp touched you in a tender spot. It matched your feelings, so you enjoyed it.
The military music went against the way you felt. You were too sad for it to lift and cheer your feelings. So it could not help but upset you.

Now suppose your heart is glowing with religious feeling. At that moment you do not want anyone to bring up a different subject. You are also not interested in anything on the same subject that is far below the level of your feelings.

Suppose you hear a cold man preach or pray. As long as he stays cold and you are warm with feeling, you are not interested. Your feelings are not fed and warmed unless he comes up to your level. If that does not happen, you are upset, and perhaps disgusted by his coldness.
This is only natural.

Suppose that, like Paul, “you have great heaviness and constant sorrow in your heart” for sinners who are dying. Suppose “the Spirit helps you in your weakness, pleading for you just as God wills, with groanings that cannot be spoken.” While you feel this way, you hear someone pray who never mentions sinners. You hear a minister preach who says very little to them, and says it in a heartless, empty way. You are not interested. Feeling as you do, you cannot be. Instead, you are hurt and upset.

Now suppose you are lukewarm, and your feelings are worldly and earthly. You hear someone encourage, pray, or preach who is very spiritual, passionate, and loving. Maybe you cling to your sins and your feelings will not rise. Maybe prejudice, or pride, or the earthly, fleshly state of your feelings makes you refuse to catch fire and take hold of the subject. Then even though you agree with every word he says, you are not pleased.
He is warmer than you are. You are annoyed by the man’s manner, his fire, and his spirit.
If your feelings stay low, then the higher he rises, the farther apart you are, and the more annoyed you become.
While your heart is wrong, the more right he is, the more he burns you. If your heart will not catch fire, the more disgusted you become.
In both of these cases, the people whose feelings are at or near the same level as the one speaking or praying will not feel bothered. They will be pleased.
Lukewarm people will listen to the dull man and say, “That was pretty good.”
Their pleasure will be small, because their feelings are low. But overall, they are pleased.
People who have no feelings at that moment will, of course, feel nothing at all.
Everyone who feels deeply will listen with sadness and pain.
These same people would listen to the passionate man with great interest.
Let him glow and blaze, and they are thrilled.
But as long as worldly, cold-hearted people refuse to rise, they cannot help being bothered and offended by his fire.
From what we have said, we can learn several things.
First, we learn why people who disagree about points of doctrine, and who belong to different church groups, will often walk together for a while in great harmony and love.
It is because they feel deeply, and they feel the same way.
While their feelings match, their differences are mostly lost or forgotten. They will walk together as long as their hearts agree.
Next, we see why new believers love to spend time with each other, and with older Christians who have the most religious feeling. These walk together because they feel the same way.
Next, we see why lukewarm people who say they are Christians, and sinners who have not repented, have the same problems with the methods used in revivals.
We often hear them complain about the way people preach and pray.
Their complaints are the same. They find fault with the same things, and they use the same arguments to back up their complaints.
The reason is that, at that time, their feelings are almost the same. It is the fire and the spirit that bother their frozen hearts.
For now they walk together, because in their feelings they agree.
Next, we see why ministers and Christians who visit revivals often raise objections at first to the methods being used. They nitpick, and sometimes they even take the side of the wicked.
The truth is, they often come from places where no revivals are happening at the time. So they often feel scolded and annoyed by the warmth and spirit they see.
The praying, preaching, and talking are warmer than they are right now.

Sometimes something holds their feelings down so that they do not enter into the spirit of the work. It may be prejudice because the revival is happening in a church group different from theirs. It may be prejudice against the preacher or the people. Or perhaps it is pride, or envy, or love of the world, or something like that.
While their hearts stay wrong, of course they will nitpick. And while their feelings stay low, the more right something is—the more spiritual and holy—the more it is bound to displease them.
Next, we see why ministers and ordinary Christians disagree about which methods are wise.

Think of a man who sees and feels the endlessly serious things of eternity. He will judge what is wise or unwise in the use of methods very differently from someone whose spiritual eyes are almost shut.

A man whose heart is breaking for sinners who are perishing will, of course, think it wise, right, and necessary to “speak very plainly.” He will think he must deal with them in a very earnest and loving way.
He would think the opposite approach was very unwise, dangerous, and even criminal.

But a man who feels very little for them, and sees little of their danger, will be happy to use very different methods, or to use them in a very different way. And of course he will have very different ideas about what is wise.
This is why we see the same person holding very different ideas about wisdom at different times. As a result, he acts very differently at those times.
In fact, a man’s ideas about which methods are wise in revivals will depend on the state of his own feelings, and on the feelings of the people around him. And to a large degree, they ought to.
After all, what would be wise in some situations would be very unwise in others.
What would be wise for one man might be very unwise for another.

What would be wise for a man when his feelings are in a certain state, and in certain circumstances, would be extremely unwise for the same man when his feelings are different and his circumstances have changed.

Suppose God’s word does not condemn a method. In most cases, it is then extremely hard to form the opinion that the method is unwise. And it is often very wrong to say so in public. That is, unless you are in a position to enter into the feelings and circumstances of the person and the people at the time the method was used.
If Christians and ministers would remember these things, a great many unkind and judgmental speeches would be avoided. And much harm to the cause of truth and goodness would be prevented.
Next, we see why lukewarm Christians and sinners are not bothered by dull preaching or praying.
It does not touch their feelings at all. So it does not upset or offend them.

So we see what happens during a revival, when cold and wicked hearts are being stirred up by plain, sharp preaching. If a dull minister is invited to preach to the people, the wicked and cold-hearted will praise his preaching.
This explains why, during times of revival, we often hear sinners and lukewarm Christians wishing their minister would preach the way he used to. They wish he would be himself again.
The reason is plain. He never used to move them. But now his fire, his spirit, and his sharpness annoy them and disturb their worldly sleep.
Next, we can learn here how much weight to give to the opinions of ministers and Christians—and to our own opinions—when our feelings are in a bad state.
How much does this man approve of what was said or done?

What does he think about the methods being used? People often ask and answer questions like these. Then they trust the answer as a great authority, without paying any attention to the state of that man’s feelings at the time.

In most cases, we are completely wrong to put much trust in our own opinions, or in other people’s opinions, about which methods are wise—unless we have evidence that our feelings, or theirs, are in the right state. If our feelings changed, we would almost certainly see things differently and change our opinion.

Christians would do well to remember and follow the resolution of President Edwards: “that he would always do what seemed most fitting to him at the times when he saw the things of religion most clearly.”
Next, we learn why churches are sometimes shaken up by revivals.

Most churches probably have at least a few hypocrites in them. Sometimes a revival has much of its mere human emotion stripped away and becomes very spiritual. Then its fire and spirit bother these people. They oppose it inside, and sometimes openly.

But sometimes only part of the true Christians in a church wake up from their sleep and become very spiritual and heavenly-minded, while the rest stay worldly and earthly in their feelings. Then the church is in danger of being torn in two.

As those who are awake become more committed, more spiritual, and more active, the others will become jealous and offended, if they will not wake up. The commitment of the others makes them feel scolded. So they will nitpick. And the higher the more spiritual people rise above them, the more annoyed they become.

The closer the committed ones come to the right state of feeling, the farther apart the two groups are. As the committed ones climb higher in holy feeling, if the others will not climb with them, those others will almost certainly sink lower. In the end they really share no feelings at all. They can no longer walk together, because they do not agree.

When a church is in this state, all its members need to search their hearts deeply. This situation is greatly to be feared and deeply to be mourned when it happens. But it is easy to explain by these simple principles of our nature. And sometimes it will happen, no matter how wisely men or angels try to prevent it.
Next, we see why ministers sometimes lose their churches because of revivals.
Sometimes, even when the minister has not acted unwisely, many people in his church and congregation will not enter into the spirit of a revival.

If his own feelings catch fire, and he cares deeply for his flock and for the honor of his Master, he will certainly press the truth on them. He will annoy them with his spirit, his sharpness, and his fire, until he offends them.

If their feelings are wrong, then the more powerfully and forcefully he pushes the truth on them, the more he will offend them—unless their feelings change. In the end, he may find it best to leave them.

All this may happen, and it may be just as right and necessary for a minister as it was for Paul. Paul left places and people when some became hardened, argued against him, spoke against God, and said evil things about the Way in front of the crowds.
Another situation may happen too. The church and people may wake up while the shepherd sleeps and refuses to wake.
This will surely turn their hearts away from him and destroy their trust in him.
In either case, they may find they cannot walk together, because they do not agree.
In the first case, the minister should obey Christ’s command and “shake the dust off his feet as a witness against them.”
In the second case, the church should shake off their sleepy minister. They are better off without him than with him.
“How terrible it will be for the shepherds who feed only themselves!
Aren’t shepherds supposed to feed the sheep?
But you do not feed the flock.
So listen, you shepherds, to the word of the Lord.

This is what the Lord God says: Look, I am against the shepherds. I will demand my flock back from them. I will stop them from feeding the flock, and the shepherds will not feed themselves anymore. I will save my flock from their mouths, so that the sheep will not be their food anymore.”
Ezekiel 34:2, 3, 9, 10. President Edwards says:

“Ministers may preach very good teaching, and work very hard and carefully. But if they show their people that they do not like this work, and are doubtful and suspicious of it, they will very likely do their people much more harm than good.

Think about what could happen if their people were allowed to believe that this great and unusual work is God’s work. The very nature of the work itself, together with the example of other towns and whatever preaching they might hear now and then, would likely do much more to wake up their people and stir them up in their faith than all the minister’s other efforts with them.

What is more, the minister’s opinion will make them suspicious of the work they hear about in other places. Because of this, the mighty hand of God that shows in it will lose its effect on their minds. But that is not all. It will also make them suspicious of anything like it that appears among themselves. They will think it is part of the same sickness that has spread so widely through the land.

And what does this really do? It makes people suspicious of all living faith. It gets people talking against it and discouraging it wherever it shows up, and knocking it on the head as fast as it rises.

We ministers, by frowning at this work year after year, will keep the sheep away from their pasture instead of doing a shepherd’s job and feeding them. In a time like this, our people would be much better off with no regular minister at all.
“Those of us who hold this sacred office need to be careful about what we do and how we behave at this time. A smaller thing in a minister will hinder God’s work than in other people.

We might be very silent, or say little about the work in our public prayers and preaching, or seem to carefully avoid speaking about it in conversation. If so, our people will take it to mean that we are suspicious of it—we who are their guides, the ones they look to for spiritual teaching. This will tend to make them suspicious too. And then the results I described earlier will follow.
It is our job more than anyone else’s to promote the work of God. So if we actually hinder it and stand in its way, how can we expect to share in its wonderful blessings?
And by keeping others from those blessings, we will keep them out of heaven. So we should think about those terrible words Christ spoke to the Jewish teachers in Matthew 23:13:
‘How terrible for you! You lock up the kingdom of heaven. You do not go in yourselves, and you do not let those who are trying to enter go in.’
If we keep the sheep away from their pasture, how will we answer to the great Shepherd? He bought the flock with his precious blood, and he has put them in our care.

I humbly ask every minister who has for so long been against this work, and has looked down on it, to think about this: has he been like Michal, who had no child? Or at least, has he been mostly barren and unsuccessful in his work? I pray to God it may not be a barrenness that lasts forever, as hers did.”
Next, we can see that worldly church members and sinners have no problem with mere human emotion.
During revivals, it is common to hear a lot of complaints against what people call “mere emotion.”

No one denies that a lot of this kind of emotion is sometimes stirred up in revivals. That is not strange. In fact, it is impossible for real religious feelings to be stirred up very much without also stirring up our natural human emotions and sensitivities. To be surprised at this, or to object to a revival because of it, is clearly foolish.
But in most cases, it is not the human emotion that offends people. As far as those emotions go, saints and sinners, and worldly and spiritual Christians, all feel exactly the same.
Sinners have as much natural emotion as saints. Cold church members have as much of it as warm, spiritual Christians.
So as far as natural emotion goes, they can all share it. And in fact, we often see that they do.

Try a style of encouraging or preaching that is designed to stir up only sympathy and natural emotion. You will soon see that cold Christians, warm Christians, and sinners all feel exactly alike. They will all cry and seem to melt, and no one will be offended. And, I might add, no one will be convinced of their sin or converted.

But change your style. Make your message more spiritual and holy. Throw yourself into it with passion and power, and appeal directly to the conscience and the heart. Their tears will soon dry up. The worldly and cold-hearted will become uneasy, and soon they will find themselves offended.

As far as natural emotion goes, they walk together, because in this they agree. But as soon as the feeling becomes spiritual and holy, they cannot go any farther together. Here they do not agree. And as long as sinners refuse to repent and cold hearts stay cold, they cannot agree.
Next, we can see why sinners who have not repented cannot like pure revivals.
It is because God is in them.
Sinners hate God. That is why God commands them to make themselves a new heart.
This is the reason—the only reason—why sinners need a new heart.

While they are ruled by “a worldly mind, which is at war with God,” it is obvious that they do hate, and must hate, everything that is like God. They hate it exactly as much as they see that it looks like him.
So we see that the more a revival has mere emotion and everything wrong stripped away, the more it is bound to offend wrong hearts.
The more of God and the less human weakness people can see in revivals, the more they will—and must—stir up the hatred of worldly hearts.
Next, we learn how to judge what look like revivals when the wicked do not oppose them.
If people ruled by a worldly mind do not oppose a revival, it must be for one of three reasons.

First, they may be so convinced of their sin that they do not dare to oppose it openly (and even then, they oppose it in their hearts). Second, there may be nothing of the Holy Spirit in these revivals. Or third—and this often happens—the methods may have been used unwisely to stir up the crowd’s emotions. Then the work of the Holy Spirit is kept out of the sinner’s sight, buried under a pile of mere emotion.
Anything that keeps the Holy Spirit’s work out of the sinner’s sight tends to prevent opposition.
And anything that lets the sinner see the hand of God will surely stir up the opposition of his unchanged heart.

So if a stirring does not bring out the opposition of the wicked and those whose hearts are wrong, then either it is not a revival at all, or it is being run in such a way that sinners do not see God’s finger in it.

So we see this: the purer and holier the methods used to promote a revival, the more they are stripped of human weakness and mere sympathy, and the more like God they are, the more they are bound to stir up the opposition of every wrong heart.
When a man’s heart is wrong about any subject, it is obvious that he cannot truly approve of what is right about that subject. That would be a contradiction.
It would be like saying he could feel both right and wrong about the same thing at the same time.

So it seems that, if all other things are equal, some methods and ways of preaching are nearest to right. They are the ones that bring out the most of the heart’s natural hatred, and that stand most directly against wrong hearts—both in what is said and in how it is said.
This shows how foolish it is to work hard at pleasing people whose feelings about religion are in a wrong state.
They cannot be pleased with anything right and holy while their hearts are in this wrong state. As we have just seen, that would be a contradiction.
This shows why so many wrong feelings are often stirred up during revivals.
Pure revivals naturally stir up wrong feelings in wrong hearts.

Revivals on earth stir up wrong feelings in hell. Whenever they come in contact with rebellious hearts, whether in the church or outside it, they will disturb that same spirit and stir up those same feelings.
Wherever the Holy Spirit comes, or is seen at work, the opposite spirit is naturally disturbed.
When saints have a great deal of right and holy feeling, it will naturally stir up a great deal of unholy and wicked feeling in all the hearts that are set on being wrong.
The more right and holy feeling there is, the more wrong and unholy feeling there will be—unless sinners and worldly church members bow down and give in.

They cannot walk together, because they do not agree. And the more holy and heavenly the saints become in their feelings and actions, the farther apart they will be. In the end, the light of eternity will set them as far apart in their feelings as heaven is from hell.

This shows what the difference between heaven and hell really is, when it comes to moral character, happiness, and misery. It is the different state of the hearts and feelings of the people who live there.
This proves beyond any argument that sinners cannot be saved unless they are born again.
In other words, by the very nature of things, it is clearly impossible for sinners to walk with saints and holy angels and be happy with them—unless their feelings are completely changed.
Sinners cannot walk with the saints here on earth.
As soon as the saints stop living “the way this world lives,” sinners think it strange that they no longer rush with them into the same wild living. So they start “speaking evil of them.”
As soon as Christians wake up and become spiritual, active, holy, and heavenly-minded, and break away from their empty and wicked friendships with the world, sinners are always upset and offended.
They try to imagine that it is something wrong in the saints, and in revivals, that offends them.
But the truth is, it is the little bit that is right in the saints—and the part of revivals that has the most of God in it—that offends them most.

If the saints were as holy as the angels, or as holy as they will be in heaven, sinners would be that much farther from sharing any feelings with them. And as saints rise in holiness and sinners sink in sin, they will move farther and farther apart forever and ever.

Lastly, I note that this shows why the lives and preaching of the prophets, of Christ and his apostles, and the revivals of the early church met with so much more violent opposition than preachers and revivals meet today. That opposition came from worldly people who claimed to be religious and from ungodly sinners.

No one can deny that the saints in those days “were cruelly mocked and whipped, and even chained and put in prison. They were stoned, sawn apart, tempted, and cut down with the sword. They wandered around in sheepskins and goatskins. They were poor, suffering, and tortured (the world was not worthy of them). They wandered in deserts and on mountains, and in caves and hideouts in the earth.”

No one does or can deny this: many people who claimed to be saints, and huge numbers of ungodly sinners, bitterly opposed the preaching of the prophets, of Christ and his apostles, and of the first ministers. They opposed it more than they oppose any preacher today.

We should not hide the fact that religious people were often the leaders of this opposition. They stirred up the Romans to crucify Jesus, and later to persecute and destroy his followers and crucify his apostles.

Even the religious teachers and scholars of the law tried to turn the crowds against the Savior and keep them from listening to his teaching. “He has a devil in him, and he is mad,” they said. “Why do you listen to him?”
They led the way in opposing the apostles in the revivals the apostles were part of.

We must also admit that those revivals made a great deal of noise in the world. The apostles were even accused of “turning the world upside down.” Sinners were often badly hardened by the preaching of Christ and his apostles. They “were filled with great anger” and opposed them so bitterly that Christ told his apostles to “leave them alone.”

In some places where the apostles preached, “some” became so “hardened” that they “argued, spoke against God, and said evil things about the Way.” So the apostles were forced to leave and go to other places. Sometimes they had to leave in very humiliating ways, barely escaping with their lives.
We do not need to be embarrassed to face these facts. They are easy to explain by the principle in our text, which this sermon has illustrated.

None of these things proves that the prophets, and Christ and his apostles, were unwise and unholy men. It does not prove that their preaching was too harsh and severe, or that revivals were being handled wrongly in those days.

The truth is this. The prophets lived much holier lives, and they were much bolder and more faithful in giving their messages. Christ was much more searching, plain, sharp, and personal in his preaching, and in his life he was completely “separate from sinners.” The apostles were very sharp and plain in dealing with sinners and with people who claimed to be saints, and they lived very holy lives of self-denial. That is why worldly church people and ungodly sinners could not walk with them.
The methods used back then to promote revivals were holier and purer than they are now.
There was less mere sympathy. There was less of that fake, smooth manner, and less of that fancy language designed to win the applause of the ungodly.

They “refused to use hidden, dishonest methods. They did not act with trickery or twist the word of God.” They preached “not with the smooth, tempting words of human wisdom,” but “very plainly.” As a result, the ungodly, both inside and outside the church, were filled with anger.
Stephen spoke in such a holy and searching way that the leaders of Israel “ground their teeth at him.”
But this does not prove that he was unwise.

Today’s revivals move much more quietly and slowly than they did on the day of Pentecost and at many other times and places. They also cause much less noise and opposition among cold church members and ungodly sinners. But that does not prove that people understand revivals better now than they did then. Nor does it prove that the ministers and Christians involved in today’s revivals are wiser than the apostles and the first Christians. To think so would show great spiritual pride in us.
And we must not say that the human heart has changed, or that God’s character has become less offensive “to the worldly mind.”

No! The truth is that the prophets, Christ, his apostles, and the early saints were holier, bolder, and more active. They were plainer and sharper in their preaching. They were less like this crazy world. In a word, they were wiser and more like heaven than we are. That is why they were hated more than we are, and why their preaching and praying offended people so much more than ours does.

In their days, revivals were freer from worldly scheming, and from the kind of management that tends to hide the bare hand of God from the sinner’s sight. That is why those revivals made so much more noise than the ones we see today. That is why they stirred up so much of earth and hell to oppose them, and why they shook the world and turned it upside down.
Back then, people knew that “people could not serve God and riches.”
They could see that it was true: “if anyone is determined to live for God in Christ Jesus, he will suffer persecution.”
People understood then that if “ministers pleased people, they were not the servants of Christ.”
The church and the world could not walk together, because back then they did not agree.

We must not become proud and imagine that we are wise and clever. We must not think we have learned how to handle worldly church members and sinners, whose “worldly mind is at war with God,” in a way that does not stir up their opposition to truth and holiness. Christ and his apostles did stir it up.

Instead, we should understand this: if they have less trouble with us—with our lives and our preaching—than they had with Christ and the apostles, it is because we are less holy, less heavenly, and less like God than they were.
If we walk with the lukewarm and the ungodly, or they walk with us, it is because we agree.
For two cannot walk together unless they agree.
Our text: “…does not seek its own interests.” — 1
Corinthians 13:5.
This means that charity, or Christian love, does not seek its own interests.
Tonight I want to prove this statement:
CARING ABOUT OUR OWN HAPPINESS MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE CANNOT GO TOGETHER WITH TRUE RELIGION.

This statement really belongs first in the series of ideas I have been working to explain in these lectures. I would have talked about it first if I had known that many people who call themselves Christians seriously doubted it.
But I can honestly say that when I started these lectures, I did not expect anyone to have a real problem with this point. So I mostly took it for granted that selfishness is not religion.
That is why I passed over this point and only tried a little to prove it.

But since then I have learned that many people who call themselves Christians believe that caring most about our own happiness is true religion. So I think I need to look at this subject more carefully. I will give you the arguments for what I believe is the truth.
To prove my point, I want to keep apart things that are different. So I will do three things:
I. Show what this statement does not mean when I say that caring most about our own happiness is not religion.
II. Show what it does mean. And
III. Try to prove it.

blocks.x: I. First, I will explain what this statement does not mean.

s: 1. The question is not whether it is right to care about our own happiness at all.
In fact, I agree, and even insist, that caring properly about our own happiness is part of our duty. We should value it as much as it is really worth when we weigh it against other interests.
God has commanded us to love our neighbor as ourselves.
This clearly makes it a duty to love ourselves, or to care about our own happiness. We are to use the same rule for ourselves that we use for others.
2. The statement does not mean that we should ignore God’s promises and warnings as they apply to us.

It is clearly right to pay attention to God’s promises and his warnings of punishment as they apply to us. But we should weigh them by how much our own interests are really worth compared with other interests.
But anyone can see that a warning against us is not as important as a warning against a great many people.
Imagine a warning of trouble aimed at you alone.
Clearly, that is not as important as a warning that included your whole family.
Now imagine it reached the whole church, or the state, or the whole nation, or the whole world.
Here it is easy to see that one person’s happiness, even though it matters a great deal, should not be put above everything else.
I am a minister.
Imagine God says to me, “If you do not do your duty, you will be sent to hell.”
That would be a terrible thing, and I should try to avoid it.
But imagine he says, “If your people do not do their duty, they will all be sent to hell. But if you do your duty faithfully, you will probably save the whole church.”
Should the fear of something bad happening to me move me as much as the fear of a whole church being sent to hell? Clearly not.
3. The question is not whether we should put our eternal good ahead of our good in this life.
I clearly teach, and so does the Bible, that we must treat our eternal good as far more important than our good in this life.
For example, the Bible tells us, “Do not work for food that spoils. Work for what lasts on into eternal life.”
This teaches that, compared with eternal life, we should not value the things of this life at all.

Our Savior teaches the same thing when he says, “Do not pile up riches for yourselves on earth, where moths and rust eat them away and thieves dig through the walls and steal them. Instead, pile up riches for yourselves in heaven, where no moth or rust eats them away and no thieves dig through or steal.”
Here we are given the same duty: to choose what lasts forever over what lasts only for this life.

Here is another example. Christ once sent out his disciples in pairs to preach and to do miracles. They came back full of joy and excitement, because they found that even the demons had to give in to their power.
“Lord, even the demons obey us.”
Jesus answers, “Do not be glad that the demons obey you. Be glad instead that your names are written in heaven.”
Here he teaches that having our names written in heaven is a greater good than having the greatest power in this world—even power over the demons themselves.
Everywhere the Bible teaches that in everything we do, we should choose eternal good over the good of this life.
But that is very different from saying that our own personal eternal good should be the highest thing we aim for.
4. The statement does not mean that hope and fear should not affect what we do.
It only means this: when hope and fear move us, we should weigh the things we hope for or fear by what they are really worth, compared with other interests.

5. The question is not whether certain people in the Bible did right. The Bible says they were moved, at least somewhat, by hope and fear. They kept their eyes on the reward to come, or on the joy that was set before them.
We agree they did right. Noah was moved by fear and built the ark.
But what mainly moved him? Was it the fear of drowning himself, or fear for his own safety?
The Bible does not say so.
He was afraid for the safety of his family. Even more, he dreaded the destruction of the whole human race and of everything that depended on it.
Whenever the Bible says that good people were moved by hope and fear, we agree.
But to use that in this argument, you would have to show that hope or fear about their own personal good was their main motive.
And the Bible never says that anywhere.
It was right for them to be moved by God’s promises and warnings.
Otherwise, they could not obey the second part of the law: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”

blocks.x: II. Next, I will show what this statement does mean: that caring about our own interests more than anything else cannot go together with true religion.

s: The question is whether caring about our own happiness more than anything else is religion.
It is whether we should fear our own damnation more than the damnation of everyone else, and more than the dishonor this would bring to God.
And it is whether we should work to secure our own happiness more than the happiness of everyone else and the glory of God.
And it is whether, if we do this, we are doing what true religion requires, or acting against true religion.
This is the real question. I want you to keep it in mind the whole time. Do not mix it up with any of the other points I have mentioned.

blocks.x: III. Now for the proof of this statement.

s: Before I prove that caring most about our own happiness cannot go together with true religion, I want to point something out. All true religion is being like God. It means acting on the same principles and reasons that he does, and feeling about different things the way he feels about them.
I do not think anyone will deny this.
In fact, no one in his right mind can deny it.
So here is my first proof of the statement:
1. Caring most about our own happiness does not follow God’s example. It makes us completely unlike him.
The Bible tells us that “God is love.”
This means that goodwill toward others is the whole of his character.
All his other moral qualities, like justice and mercy, are just different forms of this goodwill.
His love shows itself in two ways.
One is goodwill—wanting good things for others and wanting them to be happy.
The other is delight—approving of the character of others who are holy.
God’s goodwill reaches out to every being that can be happy.
It is for everyone. And toward all holy beings he shows the love of delight. In other words, God loves his neighbor as himself.
He cares about the interests of every being as much as his own, according to what each is really worth.
He seeks his own happiness, or glory, as the highest good.
But he does this not because it is his own. He does it because it is the highest good.
He is an infinite being. So the total of his happiness is infinitely greater than the total happiness of all other beings put together—or of any number of limited creatures you could imagine.
Let me give you a very simple example.
Here is a man who is kind to animals.
This man and his horse fall into a river.
Now, does true goodwill require the man to drown himself in order to get his horse out?
No. It would be true, unselfish goodwill for him to save himself and, if he has to, let his horse die. That is because his happiness is worth so much more than the horse’s happiness.
You can see this right away.
But the difference between God and all created beings is infinitely greater than the difference between a man and a horse, or between the highest angel and the smallest insect.
So God cares about the happiness of every creature exactly according to what it is really worth.
And unless we do the same, we are not like God.
If we are like God, we must see God’s happiness and glory the way he does. That is, we must see them as the highest good, above everything else in the universe.
And if we want our own happiness more than God’s happiness, we are infinitely unlike God.
2. Aiming at our own happiness above everything cannot go together with true religion, because it goes against the spirit of Christ.
We are told that “if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.”
And the Bible says again and again that Jesus, as a man, did not seek his own interests. It says that he did not seek his own glory, and other things like that.
What was he seeking?
Was it his own personal salvation?
No. Was it his own personal happiness?
No. It was the glory of his Father and the good of the whole universe, through saving people.
He came on a mission of pure goodwill. He came to do good for the kingdom of God, not to do good for himself.
This was “the joy that was set before him.” Because of it “he endured the cross and thought nothing of the shame.”
It was the great good he could do by giving himself completely to work and suffer so that people could be saved.
3. Making our own happiness the main thing we chase goes against the law of God.
I have mentioned this before. But I am coming back to it so that my proof here will be complete.
The whole law comes down to this: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. And love your neighbor as yourself.”
This is the great thing God requires: goodwill toward God and toward people.
The first thing is to truly love God’s happiness and glory more than anything else. That is because it is so infinitely lovely and worth wanting, and it really is the highest good.
Some people have argued that it is not our duty to seek God’s happiness, because his happiness is already safe.

Now imagine that the king of England does not need me at all, and his happiness is safe without me. Does that make it any less my duty to wish him well, to want him to be happy, and to be glad about his happiness?
God is happy in himself and does not need his creatures. But is that a reason for us not to love his happiness and be glad about it? How strange!
Again, the terms of God’s law require us to delight in God, because he is holy—infinitely holy.
Again, this law requires us to show the same goodwill to others that we show to ourselves. That is, we must seek both their interests and our own, according to what each is really worth.
Which of you is doing this?
And we are required to show the love of delight toward those who are good and holy.
So we see what God’s law comes down to. We must show goodwill toward God and all beings, according to what each is really worth. And we must delight in all who are holy.
Now here is what I say: to care about our own happiness above all, or to make it our highest goal, goes against that law. It goes against both its words and its spirit. And
4. It goes against the gospel just as much as it goes against the law.

In the chapter our text comes from, the apostle begins like this: “I may speak in the languages of men and of angels. But if I do not have charity, I have become like a clanging piece of brass or a jingling cymbal.
I may have the gift of prophecy and understand all mysteries and all knowledge. I may have so much faith that I could move mountains. But if I do not have charity, I am nothing.”
Here the word charity means love.
In the original language, it is the same word that is translated love.
“I may give away everything I own to feed the poor. I may even give my body to be burned. But if I do not have charity, it does me no good at all.”
Now, notice this! He could not have used stronger words to say that charity, or goodwill, is necessary for true religion.
See how he puts up guards on every side, so that no one can possibly mistake what he means.
If a person does not have true charity, he is nothing.
Then he goes on to describe what this true charity is like.

“Charity puts up with a lot for a long time and is kind. Charity does not envy. Charity does not brag about itself and is not full of pride. It does not behave improperly. It does not seek its own interests. It is not easily made angry. It thinks no evil. It is not glad about wickedness, but is glad about the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.”
Here you see that one main mark of this love is that charity “does not seek its own interests.”
Notice that! If this is true religion, and there is no religion without it, then one mark of true religion is that it “does not seek its own interests.”
Some of you have Bibles with cross-references in the margins. You can follow those references and find a great many passages that clearly teach the same thing.
Remember the passages I quoted in my last lecture.
I will mention just one of them: “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it.”
Here you see it stated as a fixed rule of how God governs: if a person aims above all at his own interests, he will lose them.
The same thing is taught in the tenth chapter of this letter, verse 24: “No one should seek his own interests. Instead, everyone should seek another person’s wealth.”
If you look at this passage, you will see that the word wealth is printed in italics. That shows it is a word the translators added. It is not in the Greek.
They could just as well have used the word happiness, or welfare, instead of wealth.
It is the same in verse 33: “In the same way, I please everybody in every way. I am not looking for what benefits me, but for what benefits many people, so that they can be saved.”
So I say that making our own interests the main thing we chase goes against the gospel just as much as it goes against the law.
5. It goes against conscience.
The conscience of all people everywhere has decided that caring about our own happiness above everything is not goodness.
People have always known that serving God and doing good to others is right. And they have always known that seeking their own personal interests above everything is not right.

They have always thought it low and shameful for people to make their own happiness their highest goal. That is why we see people work so hard to hide their selfishness and to look as if they care about others.
Anyone can see that it is sinful to put his own happiness above other, more important interests—unless his conscience has been strangely dulled by sin or twisted by false teaching.
6. It goes against clear thinking.
Clear thinking teaches us to value everything according to what it is really worth.
God does this, and we should do the same.
God gave us the ability to reason for this very purpose: so that we could weigh and compare how much different things are worth.
It makes a joke of reason to deny that it teaches us to value things according to what they are really worth.
And if that is true, then aiming at our own interests and putting them first, as our highest goal, goes against reason.
7. It goes against common sense.
What has the common sense of humanity decided about this?
Look at what people’s common sense says about what we call patriotism.
No one was ever thought of as a true patriot for fighting for his country if his goal was to serve his own interests.
Imagine it turned out that his goal in fighting was to get himself crowned king. Would anyone give him credit for being a patriot?
No. Everyone agrees that it is patriotism when a man is unselfish, like Washington, and fights for his country for his country’s sake.
The common sense of humanity has stamped its disapproval on the attitude that seeks its own things. It condemns putting our own interests ahead of the greater interests of others.
It is clear that everyone sees it this way.
If not, why does everyone want so much to look unselfish?
8. It goes against the way our minds are made.
I do not mean that the way we are made makes it impossible for us to seek our own happiness as our highest goal.
But we are made in such a way that if we do this, we can never reach it.
As I said in an earlier lecture, happiness is the satisfaction of desire.
We must want something, and then get the thing we want.
Now imagine a man who wants his own happiness. What he wants will always stay just out of reach, like his shadow. The faster he chases it, the faster it runs away.
Happiness is always tied to getting the thing we want.
Suppose I want a thousand dollars.
That is the thing my desire is fixed on. When I get it, that desire is satisfied, and I am happy—at least as far as satisfying this desire can make me happy.
But suppose I want the thousand dollars so I can buy a watch, some clothes, and things like that. Then my desire is not satisfied until I get those things.
But now imagine that the thing I wanted was my own happiness.
Then getting the thousand dollars does not make me happy, because that is not what my desire was fixed on.
And getting the watch and the clothes and the other things will not make me happy either, because they do not satisfy my desire.
God has set things up, and given our minds such laws, that people can never gain happiness by chasing it.
The very way we are made clearly shows that it is our duty to have unselfish goodwill.
In fact, God has made it impossible for people to be happy except to the degree that they are unselfish.
Picture two men walking down the street together.
They come upon a man who has just been run over by a cart. He is lying there covered in his own blood.
They pick him up, carry him to the doctor, and get him help.
Now it is clear that their satisfaction is as great as their desire to see him helped.
If one of them felt very little and cared very little about the poor man’s suffering, he will feel very little satisfaction.
But if his desire to see the man helped was so strong that it was agony, his satisfaction would be just as great.
Now imagine a third person who had no desire to help the injured man. Helping him certainly could not give that person any satisfaction.
He could walk right past him and watch him die.
So he feels no satisfaction at all.
So you see, our happiness is exactly as great as our desires are satisfied by getting the things we want.
Notice this too: for the happiness of a satisfied desire to be complete, the desire itself must be good.
If the desire is selfish, the satisfaction will be mixed with pain, because the mind is at war with itself.
We know all this is true because we are aware of it inside ourselves. That is the very strongest kind of evidence we can have.
And anyone who denies it is accusing God of acting foolishly—as if he had made us in a way that would not let us be happy when we obey him.
9. Making our own interests our highest goal also works against our own happiness.
This follows from what I just said.
People may enjoy a certain kind of pleasure, but not true happiness.
Any pleasure that does not come from satisfying a good desire is a false thing that fools us.
Everyone wants happiness so badly. So why doesn’t everyone find it? The reason is that they are chasing IT.
If they would seek the glory of God and the good of the universe as their highest goal, IT would chase them.
10. It works against the happiness of everyone together.
Imagine that each person aims at his own happiness as his main goal. Then all these interests will clash and crash into each other. When everyone is selfish, war and chaos everywhere will follow.
11. To say that caring most about our own interests is true religion goes against the experience of every real saint.
I say it plainly: every real saint knows that his greatest happiness comes from getting outside himself and caring about the glory of God and the good of others.
If he does not know this, he is not a saint.
12. It also goes against the experience of everyone who once had a selfish religion, then found out their mistake and got true religion.
This happens often.
I think I have known hundreds of cases.
Some members of this church have recently made this discovery.
And they can all tell you that they now know from experience that goodwill is true religion.
13. It goes against the experience of everyone who has not repented.
Every sinner who has not repented knows that he is aiming above all at getting ahead for himself. And he knows that he does not have true religion.
The very thing his conscience condemns him for is this: he is looking after his own interests instead of the glory of God.
Now let’s turn the page for a moment. Let’s suppose that caring most about our own happiness really is true religion. Then see what would follow.
1. Then it would follow that God is not holy.
That is, if caring most about our own interests, just because they are our own, is true religion, then it would follow that God is not holy.
God cares about his own happiness. But that is because it is the greatest good, not because it is his own.
But he is love, or goodwill. So if goodwill is not true religion, God’s nature would have to change.
2. The law of God would have to be changed.

If caring most about our own happiness is religion, then the law should say, “Love yourself with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. And love God and your neighbor infinitely less than yourself.”
3. The gospel would have to be turned upside down.
Instead of saying, “Whether you are eating or drinking, or doing anything at all, do everything to bring glory to God,” it would say, “Do everything for your own happiness.”

Instead of “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it,” we would find it saying, “Whoever is extremely anxious to save his own life will save it. But whoever is full of goodwill, and willing to lose his life for the good of others, will lose it.”
4. People’s consciences would have to be changed. They would have to speak up for selfishness, and condemn and reject anything that looks like unselfish goodwill.

5. Clear thinking would have to be made to stop weighing things by what they are really worth. Instead, it would have to decide that our own small interests are worth more than the greatest interests of God and the universe.
6. Common sense would have to decide that true patriotism means every man seeking his own interests instead of the good of everyone, and each one trying to build himself up as high as he can.
7. The way human beings are made would have to be turned upside down.
If extreme selfishness is goodness, then human beings were made wrong.
We are made in such a way that we can be happy only by having goodwill toward others.
And if this teaching is true—that religion means seeking our own happiness as the highest good—then the more religion a person has, the more miserable he is.
8. And the whole structure of society would have to be changed.
Right now, the good of the community depends on how much each person cares about the good of everyone.
If this teaching holds, that would have to change. Then the good of everyone would be served best when every person is scrambling for his own interests without caring about the interests of others.
9. The experience of the saints would have to be turned upside down.

Right now they find that the more goodwill they have, the more religion and the more happiness they have. Instead, they would have to say that the more they aim at their own good, the more they enjoy religion and God’s favor.
10. And people who have not repented would have to say that they are extremely happy in their extreme selfishness, and that they find true happiness in it.
I will not take this proof any further. It would start to look as if I were not being serious.
If anything can be proved at all, then this has been fully proved: aiming at our own happiness above everything cannot go together with true religion.
I. We see why so few people find happiness, even though everyone is chasing it.
The fact is plain to see.
Here is the reason. Most people do not know what true happiness is. They are looking for it in things that can never give it.
They do not find it because they are chasing it.
If they would turn around and chase holiness, happiness would chase them.
If they would become unselfish and put all their effort into doing good, they could not help being happy.
If they choose happiness as their goal, it runs away from them.
True happiness is the satisfaction of good desires. If people would set out to glorify God and do good, they would find it.
The only people who never find it, in this world or the world to come, are the ones who make it their goal.
II. The way God made the human mind and the universe gives us a beautiful picture of how God arranges things.
Imagine that people could find happiness only by chasing their own happiness.

Then each person would have only the happiness he had gotten for himself. All the happiness in the universe would just be the total of what each person had gotten—minus all the pain and misery caused when people’s interests clash.
Now notice this! God has set things up so that while each person works hard for the happiness of others, his own happiness is made safe and complete.
So the total happiness in the universe is far, far greater than it would have been if selfishness had been the law of Jehovah’s kingdom!
That is because everyone who obeys God’s law fully secures his own happiness through his goodwill. And the happiness of everyone together grows by as much as each person receives from all the others.
Many people say, “Who will take care of my happiness if I don’t?
If I am supposed to care only about my neighbor’s interests and neglect my own, none of us will be happy.”
That would be true if caring about your neighbor’s happiness took away from your own.
But if your happiness comes from doing good and making others happy, then the more you do for others, the more you add to your own happiness.
III. When I announced the topic of this lecture, I avoided using the word selfishness. I was afraid it would sound insulting.
But now I say it clearly: caring most about our own interests is selfishness, and nothing else.
If God cared most about his own interests just because they are his own, that would be selfishness in God.
And it is selfishness in people.
So anyone who says that caring most about our own interests is true religion is saying that selfishness is true religion.
IV. If selfishness is goodness, then goodwill is sin.
They are exact opposites. They cannot both be goodness.
When a man sets his own interests above God’s interests—when he prefers them and sets them against God’s interests—that is selfishness.
And if that is goodness, then Jesus Christ, by seeking the good of humanity the way he did, turned away from what is good.
Who would dare to claim that?
V. People who put their own interests first and still think they have true religion are deceived.
I say this very seriously, because I believe it is true. I would say it even if it were the last thing I said before going to face God’s judgment.
Dear listener, whoever you are, if you are doing this, you are not a Christian.
Do not call this being judgmental.
I am not being judgmental.
I would not condemn anyone.
But as surely as God is true, and as surely as your soul is going to face judgment, you do not have the religion of the Bible.
VI. Some will ask here, “What? Are we not supposed to care about our happiness at all? And if so, how are we supposed to tell whether we care about it most or not?”
I do not say that.
I say you may care about it according to what it is really worth.
Now I ask you, is this really hard to figure out in practice?
I appeal to what you know inside yourself.
If you are honest, you cannot help knowing what you care about most.
On one side are your own interests. On the other side are God’s glory and the good of the universe. Are these so evenly balanced in your mind that you cannot tell which one you prefer?
That is impossible! You should be as sure that you prefer God’s glory to your own interests as you are sure that you exist. If you are not, you can take it for granted that you are completely wrong.
VII. You see why the joy of so many people who claim to be religious depends on their proofs that they are saved.
These people are always hunting for proof. And their joy goes up and down as that proof changes.
Now notice this! If they really cared about the glory of God and the good of humanity, their joy would not depend on their proofs.
People who are completely selfish may enjoy religion a lot. But it is the joy of looking forward to something.
They like the idea of going to heaven.
But those who get outside themselves and are full of pure goodwill have heaven in their hearts right now.
VIII. You see from this that all of you who had no peace and joy in religion until you had a hope of being saved are deceived.
Maybe I can describe what happened to you.
You were woken up spiritually. And you were upset, as you had reason to be, because you were afraid of going to hell.
After a while, maybe while you were praying, or while someone was talking with you, your distress went away.
You thought your sins were forgiven.
A flash of joy went through your mind and warmed your heart until it glowed. You took that as proof, and that made you even happier.
How very different the experience of a true Christian is!
His peace does not depend on his hope. Real surrender to God and real goodwill bring peace and joy all by themselves, apart from his hope.
Imagine a man in prison who has been sentenced to be hanged the next day.
He is very upset. He paces back and forth in his cell, waiting for the day to come.
After a while a messenger comes with a pardon.
He grabs the paper and holds it up to the dim light coming through the bars of his window. He reads the word PARDON. He almost faints with emotion, and he jumps for joy.
He believes the paper is real.
Now suppose it turns out that the paper is a fake.
Suddenly all his joy is gone.
It is the same with a person who is deceived.
He was afraid of going to hell. So of course he is happy if he believes he is forgiven.
If the devil told him so, and he believed it, his joy would be just as great—as long as he kept believing it—as if it were real.
True Christian joy does not depend on proofs.
The true Christian puts himself into God’s hands with such trust, and that very act gives him peace.
He had a terrible fight with God. But all at once he stops arguing and gives in. He says, “God will do what is right. Let God’s will be done.”
Then he begins to pray. He is humbled. His heart melts before God. And that very act brings sweet, calm, heavenly joy.
Maybe he has not even thought about having a hope.
He may go for hours, or even a day or two, full of joy in God, without thinking about his own salvation.
If you ask him whether he has a hope, he never even thought about it.
His joy does not depend on believing that he is forgiven. It comes from a state of mind that accepts God’s rule.
With a mind like that, he cannot help being happy.
Now let me ask you: which religion do you have?

If you practice true religion, imagine that God put you into hell and let you keep loving God above all, and loving your neighbor as yourself. That state of mind itself could not go together with being miserable.
I want you to understand this completely.
These people who chase after a hope will always be disappointed.
If you run after hope, you will never have a hope worth anything.
But if you pursue holiness, then hope and peace and joy will come naturally.
Is your religion a love of holiness—a love of God and of people’s souls?
Or is it only a hope?
IX. You see why sinners who are worried about their souls do not find peace.
They are looking at their own guilt and danger.
They see God as someone who punishes, and they shrink back from his terrors.
This will make it impossible for them ever to find peace.
While they look at God’s anger, which makes them wither and shake, they cannot love him. They hide from him.
Worried sinners, let me tell you a secret.
If you keep looking at only that side of God’s character, it will drive you to despair. And despair does not go together with true surrender to God.

You should look at his whole character. See the reasons why you should love him. Throw yourself on him without holding anything back and without any distrust. Instead of shrinking back from him, come straight to him and say, “O Father in heaven, you are not stern and unbending. You are the ruler of all, but you are good. I accept your rule, and I give myself to you—everything I have and everything I am, body and soul, for now and for eternity.”
My next lecture will be about the difference between submitting to God under the law and submitting to God through the gospel—or between the religion of the law and the religion of faith.
And let me point out that when I started preaching about selfishness in religion, I never dreamed anyone would think it was a controversial subject at all.
I do not like arguing. To me, calling this a controversial subject makes as little sense as calling the teaching that God exists controversial.
This question is extremely important. We should weigh the arguments and decide according to the word of God.

Soon we will all stand together before God’s judgment seat. You must decide whether you will go there with selfishness in your hearts, or with that unselfish goodwill that does not seek its own interests. Will you be honest now?
Because as surely as God is true, if you are seeking your own interests, you will soon be in hell—unless you repent.
Oh, be honest! Put aside your prejudice, and act with eternity in mind.
“God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son. Whoever believes in him will not be lost but will have life that lasts forever.” — John 3:16
Sin is the most costly thing in the whole universe.
Nothing else costs so much.
Whether it is forgiven or not, its cost is endlessly great.
When sin is forgiven, the cost falls mainly on the great one who took our place to pay for it. When it is not forgiven, the cost must fall on the guilty sinner himself.
Sin is real. People everywhere experience it, and people everywhere see it.
There is sin in the human race everywhere, and it is terribly bad.
Sin means breaking a law that is endlessly important. This law was designed and fitted to bring about the greatest good for the whole universe.
By its very nature, obeying this law is necessary for the good of every creature.
Without obedience, there could be no happiness even in heaven.
Since sin breaks such an important law, it cannot be taken lightly.
No government can afford to treat disobedience as a small thing. Everything depends on obedience—the whole well-being of the government and of everyone it rules.
The more valuable the things at stake, the more necessary it is to protect the law and to punish disobedience.
God must not do anything that dishonors his law.
People have already dishonored it by disobeying it. So God has all the more reason to stand by his law and win back its honor.
The worst dishonor you can do to a law is to reject it, disobey it, and look down on it.
Sinful people have done all of this.

This law is not only good. It is truly needed for the happiness of everyone who lives under it. So the most necessary thing of all is that the Lawgiver should defend his law and show that it is right.
He absolutely must do it.
That is why sin has cost God’s government so much.

There are only two choices. Either the law’s punishment must be carried out, and that would cost the well-being of the whole human race. Or God must put up with the worst results of people disrespecting his law—and in some form, those results would also cost a huge amount.
Take any human government as an example.
Suppose people reject and dishonor the fair and necessary laws it makes.
Then the broken law must be honored by carrying out its punishment. If not, something else must be suffered that costs just as much, and probably much more.
Breaking the law must cost happiness somewhere, and a great deal of it.
In God’s government, it was judged wise to provide a substitute—someone to take the sinner’s place. This substitute would save the sinner and still honor the law.
Once this was decided, the next big question was: How will the cost be paid?
The Bible tells us how this question was actually answered.
It was done by a kind of volunteer sign-up—should I call it that? Or should I call it a gift?
Whatever we call it, it was an offering given freely.
Who will put his name at the top of the list of givers?
Who will start, when so much has to be raised?
Who will make the first sacrifice?
Who will take the first step in such a huge project?
The Bible tells us.
It began with the Father, who is infinite.
He made the first great gift.
To begin with, he gave his only Son. And after giving him first, he freely gives everything else the situation needs.
First he gave his Son to make the payment for sin that the law required. Then he gave and sent his Holy Spirit to take charge of this work.
The Son, for his part, agreed to stand in for sinners. He did this so he could honor the law by suffering in their place.

He poured out his blood. He freely offered a whole life of suffering on the altar. He did not hide his face when people spat on him, or his back when they whipped him. He did not pull back from the worst insults that wicked people could pile on him.
In the same way, the Holy Spirit gives himself without stopping to the most self-sacrificing efforts, to reach this great goal.

It would have been very quick and simple for God just to turn his hand against the wicked people of our race and send them all straight down to hell. He did that once with certain angels who “did not keep their first place.”
A rebellion broke out in heaven.
God did not put up with it for long around his high throne.

But with human beings he took a different path. He did not send them all to hell. Instead, he planned a huge set of steps to win people’s souls back to obedience and to heaven. This plan involved the most amazing self-denial and self-sacrifice.
Who was this great gift for?
“God so loved the world.” This means the whole human race.
Here, “the world” cannot mean just one part of it. It means the whole race.
The Bible shows it, and so does the very nature of the matter: the atonement—Christ’s payment for sin—must have been made for the whole world.

Here is why. If it had not been made for the whole race, no person could ever know that it was made for him. Then no one could believe in Christ in the sense of receiving the blessings of the atonement by faith. Suppose the gift were only for some people, and no one knew who they were. Then the whole gift would fail, because no one could have a sensible faith to receive it.
Imagine a rich man writes a will. He leaves certain property to certain people no one knows. The only description he gives of them is the name “the elect.”

That is the only way they are described. Everyone agrees that the man who wrote the will had exact people in mind. But he left no description of them that anyone could understand—not the people themselves, not the courts, not anyone alive.
A will like that is completely worthless. It cannot be used at all.
No one alive could claim anything under such a will. It would not help even if these chosen people were described as people who live in Oberlin.
The will does not include everyone who lives in Oberlin, and it does not say which ones. So everything is lost.
Everyone has an equal claim, but no one has a clear claim. So no one can inherit anything.
If the atonement were made like that, no one alive would have any good reason to believe he was one of the chosen before he received the gospel.
So he would have no right to believe and to receive its blessings by faith.
In fact, if that were true, the atonement would be completely useless—unless God gave a special message to each person it was meant for.
But here is how it really is. The simple fact that a person belongs to Adam’s race—that he is human, born of a woman—is all that is needed.
That puts him inside the circle.
He is part of the world that God gave his Son for, so that whoever would believe in him would not be lost but would have life that lasts forever.
What moved God’s heart to give this great gift was love—love for the world.
God loved the world so much that he gave his Son to die for it.
God loved the rest of the universe too. But this gift of his Son came from his love for our world.
It is true that in this great act God also took care of the interests of the whole universe.
He was careful not to do anything that would make his law seem even a little less sacred.

He very carefully made sure that no one would misunderstand how much he values his law. He also wanted no one to misunderstand how much he cares about obedience and happiness among all the thinking creatures of his universe.
He meant, once and for all, to remove the danger that any thinking, choosing creature would be tempted to think little of the moral law.
There is more. God gave up his Son to die not only because he loved souls. He also did it out of respect for the spirit of the law that comes from his own eternal reason.
This is where his plan to give up his Son began.
The law of his own reason must be honored and kept sacred.
He may not do anything that goes against its spirit.
He must do everything possible to keep people from sinning and to win the trust and love of those he rules.
He held these great goals so sacred that he would rather bathe his Son in his own blood than put the good of the universe in danger.
Without any doubt, it was love and concern for the highest good of the universe that led him to sacrifice his own dear Son.
Next, let us think carefully about what kind of love this is.
The verse puts special weight on this: “God so loved.” His love was of such a kind—so wonderful and so special—that it led him to give up his only Son to die.
Clearly, these words mean more than just that his love was great.
His love is very special in its character.

If we do not understand this, we may fall into the strange mistake of the Universalists. They are always talking about God’s love for sinners. But their ideas about what this love is like never lead anyone to repent or to become holy.

They seem to think of this love as simple niceness. They think of God only as a very kind, easygoing being whom nobody needs to fear. Ideas like that do not help anyone become holy at all. In fact, they do the very opposite.
Only when we understand what kind of love this is do we feel its moral power pushing us toward holiness.
Someone could fairly ask this: If God loved the world with a love that was simply great, and nothing more, why didn’t he just save the whole world without sacrificing his Son?
That question is enough to show that the little word “so” has a deep meaning. It should lead us to study that meaning carefully.
1. This love is not the kind that takes pleasure in how good someone is. It was not delight in the character of the human race.
That could not be, because there was nothing lovable in their character.
If God had loved such a race by taking pleasure in them, it would have been an endless disgrace to him.
2. It was not just an emotion or a feeling.
It was not a blind urge, even though many people seem to think it was.
People often seem to think God acted the way people do when strong feelings carry them away.
But there would be nothing good or right in that.
A man might give away everything he owns because of a blind rush of feeling, and not be any better a person because of it.
But saying this does not mean there is no emotion at all in the love that wants good for others, or in God’s love for a lost world.
He did have emotion, but not only emotion.

In fact, the Bible teaches everywhere that God’s love for people lost in their sins was a father’s love—the love of a father for his children. In this case, they were rebellious, stubborn children who had run away and wasted everything.
Of course, the deepest compassion must be mixed into this love.
3. On Christ’s side, as the one who stands between God and people, this love was a father’s love.
“He is not ashamed to call them his brothers.”
In one way he is acting for his brothers, and in another way for his children.
The Father gave him up for this work. So of course the Father shares in the love that fits these relationships.
4. This love must be completely unselfish. God had nothing to hope for and nothing to fear. He had nothing to gain from his children if they were saved.
